name: Vercel AI SDK
note: The standard if you're building in React/Next.js.
good: Abstracts streaming perfectly. RSC integration is magic. Easy switching between providers.
bad: Heavily ties you to Vercel's ecosystem and Next.js paradigms. Doing things outside their happy path (like custom memory management) is painful.

name: LangChain (JS/Python)
note: The monolith everyone uses then complains about.
good: Incredible amount of integrations. If a tool exists, LangChain has a loader for it.
bad: Overly complex abstractions. You spend more time fighting LangChain classes than writing AI logic. Bloated.

name: LlamaIndex
note: Better than LangChain if your primary focus is RAG.
good: Excellent data ingestion and indexing strategies. Actually understands how chunking should work.
bad: Still suffers from heavy abstraction. Hard to debug when retrieval fails.

name: LiteLLM
note: A lifesaver for standardizing API calls.
good: Call 100+ LLMs using the OpenAI format. Simple proxy server setup. Great for cost tracking.
bad: Sometimes lags behind provider-specific feature releases (like new tool calling formats).

name: Instructor
note: The only right way to do structured outputs in Python.
good: Uses Pydantic directly. No new abstractions to learn. Just works.
bad: Python and JS versions have feature parity issues. Relies heavily on OpenAI's specific tool calling reliability.

name: Semantic Kernel
note: Microsoft's take on LangChain. Enterprise heavy.
good: C# support is first-class. Integrates well with Azure.
bad: Verbose. Documentation assumes you are building enterprise software with 10 layers of architecture.

name: Braintrust
note: Eval framework that actually makes sense.
good: Focuses on code-based evals rather than UI clicking. Great TypeScript support.
bad: Pricing scales aggressively with usage. Not a full execution harness, just evals/logging.

name: Haystack
note: A mature alternative to LangChain for search/RAG.
good: Clearer pipeline architecture than LangChain. Good document stores.
bad: Smaller community means fewer random integrations. Python only.
